title: Tenosynovitis (tendon sheath inflammation)
intro: Tenosynovitis is inflammation of the protective sheath that surrounds a tendon, most commonly in the wrist, hand and fingers. It causes pain, swelling and sometimes difficulty moving, and may follow overuse, injury or infection. Treatment ranges from rest and splinting to injections and, occasionally, surgery.

sections.heading: What tendon sheaths do
paragraphs: Tendons slide through sheaths filled with a lubricating fluid, which lets them move smoothly over bones and joints. When a sheath becomes inflamed or thickened, the tendon cannot glide freely, causing pain and sometimes a catching or snapping sensation.

sections.heading: Common types
paragraphs: De Quervain's tenosynovitis affects the tendons on the thumb side of the wrist and is common in new parents and people who do repetitive thumb movements. Trigger finger occurs when a finger catches or locks in a bent position because the tendon thickens and sticks in its sheath. Other forms occur around the ankle and foot. Rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes increase the risk.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Pain and tenderness along the tendon, swelling, warmth and stiffness, pain with gripping or thumb movement, and in trigger finger a click or locking, especially in the morning. Pain that worsens with movement and relief with rest suggests overuse. Fever, spreading redness, severe pain on straightening a finger and a sausage-shaped swollen finger suggest infection and need urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Rest from provoking activity, a splint to support the area, ice, and anti-inflammatory painkillers or gels often help. Corticosteroid injections around the tendon sheath are effective in many people, particularly for de Quervain's and trigger finger. Hand therapy provides exercises and advice on movement. Infections need antibiotics and sometimes surgical drainage.

sections.heading: Surgery and prevention
paragraphs: If symptoms persist or recur, a small operation releases the tight sheath so that the tendon moves freely, usually under local anaesthetic with a short recovery. Prevent problems by varying repetitive tasks, taking breaks, using ergonomic tools and avoiding sustained forceful gripping.

examples.title: Protecting the wrist
examples.text: Imagine your wrist hurts when lifting your baby. You could wear a thumb splint for a few weeks, adjust how you hold your baby and ask about injection if pain persists.

examples.title: Spotting a warning sign
examples.text: Suppose a finger becomes red, swollen and very painful to straighten. You might seek urgent care, as it may be an infection.
